item.content:encoded:
Git basics (Version control with Git)

Git from zero: 12 picture cards with native audio, the traps people actually fall into, real questions and 24 version-control words.

The big picture

Git is a time machine for your files. Every commit is a snapshot you can return to, compare or hand to someone else — and none of it needs the internet.

  • Time machine: Every save point stays forever
  • Choose what to save: Staging picks the changes for you
  • Snapshots have IDs: A short hash names every commit
  • Parallel lines: Branches let ideas grow apart safely
  • Conflicts are normal: Two edits, one line — you choose
  • Shared backup: The remote holds everyone's work

Text

Start · Make a repo
git init turns this folder into a repository that Git can watch. Everything Git remembers lives inside one hidden folder called .git.
git init — run once in the project root Delete .git and all history is gone — the files stay

Work · Track changes
When you are lost, run git status — it says where you are and what changed. git diff shows every line that changed before you decide anything. git add puts changes in the staging area — the waiting list for the next snapshot.
git status git diff · git diff --staged git add login.py (or git add . for everything)

Save · Commit snapshots
git commit saves the staged changes as one snapshot, with a message that says why. git log walks you backwards through every snapshot, newest first. Undo is never scary here: git restore brings a file back from the last snapshot.
git commit -m "fix login timeout" git log --oneline --graph git restore login.py · undo a commit: git reset --soft HEAD~1

Branch · Parallel work
A branch is its own line of work, so an experiment can't break main. Merging folds one branch's snapshots into another; a conflict is just Git asking who wins.
git switch -c new-feature git switch main · git merge new-feature

Share · Push and pull
A remote is the shared copy of your repo, usually on GitHub — everyone's work lives there. Clone copies a whole repo with history; push sends your commits out; pull brings other people's in.
origin = the default name of your remote git clone <url> · git push · git pull --rebase

Q&A

Traps

Q. I ran git add . and committed everything — including my secrets.
A. Untrack it now: git rm --cached .env, put it in .gitignore, commit. If the repo was ever pushed, rotate the secret — history keeps old copies forever.

Q. I work straight on main because branching feels like extra work.
A. Open a branch before every change: git switch -c fix-login. Merging your own small branch takes seconds and keeps mistakes off main.

Q. I thought git pull just downloads files.
A. Pull downloads other people's commits AND merges them into your work — that is where conflicts come from. Use git fetch to look first, merge when ready.

Q. I deleted a commit by mistake — it is gone forever?
A. Almost never. git reflog lists every position HEAD has held; find the old hash and reset hard back to it. (git reflog · then git reset --hard <hash>)

Real questions

Q. How do I undo my last commit but keep the changes?
A. git reset --soft HEAD~1 — the commit disappears and your changes wait in the staging area.

Q. What exactly is HEAD?
A. HEAD is where you are right now: which branch, on which commit. Undo commands are really about moving it.

Q. My push was rejected. What now?
A. The remote has commits you don't. Run git pull --rebase, fix any conflicts, then git push again.

Q. A merge conflict appeared. Walk me through it.
A. Open the marked files, keep the lines you want, delete Git's marker lines, then git add each file and commit. (markers look like: <<<<<<< HEAD / ======= / >>>>>>> other-branch)

Q. How do I stop tracking a file without deleting it?
A. Run git rm --cached for that file, add it to .gitignore, commit. The file stays on your disk. (git rm --cached <file> · then list it in .gitignore)

When you are stuck

Read git status again — it usually names the exact next command. (Git's own hint line is the map.)

git log --oneline --graph --all shows where every branch really is. (See the whole map before touching anything.)

git reflog finds commits you thought were lost. (The safety net for undo disasters.)

Type git help, then any command name, to read its manual page offline. (The docs live in your terminal.)

Vocabulary (24)

The objects
repository: The project folder plus all its history, inside .git
working directory: Your actual files, the ones you edit
staging area: The prepared set of changes for the next commit; also called the index
commit: One saved snapshot of the project with a unique hash
HEAD: A pointer to where you are now — branch and commit
branch: An independent line of commits
remote: A shared copy of the repository on another server
tag: A permanent name pinned to one commit, like v1.0

The actions
init: Create a new repository in this folder
clone: Copy an existing repository with its full history
stage (add): Put changes into the staging area
commit: Save the staged changes as a snapshot
push: Send your commits to the remote
pull: Fetch the remote's commits and integrate them
fetch: Download the remote's commits without touching your work
merge: Combine two branches' histories into one
rebase: Replay your commits on top of another line

Signals and files
.gitignore: A list of paths Git should never track
diff: The exact lines added or removed between two versions
conflict: Two changes to the same place that Git cannot decide for you
origin: The default name of the remote you cloned from
upstream: The remote branch your branch tracks
commit message: One line saying why the change exists
reflog: Local history of every place HEAD has been
